questions.q: In a two-tier compilation model, what does the compiler itself output?
choices: Machine-level binary instructions for the target computer
Intermediate VM code (bytecode) that runs on an abstract virtual machine
Assembly code for the target computer
A list of OS calls for the hardware to execute
questions.explain: The compiler emits VM code for an abstract virtual machine. A separate VM translator then turns that VM code into the machine language of each host platform.

questions.q: Compared with one-tier compilation, which of these are drawbacks of the two-tier model?
choices: It needs a separate VM translator for each target hardware platform
It tends to produce less efficient machine code
It needs a separate full compiler for each target hardware platform
The compiled program can run on only one platform
questions.explain: Two-tier compilation costs one VM translator per platform (much simpler to write than a compiler) and somewhat less efficient code. In return you get 'compile once, run everywhere'. Needing a whole compiler per platform is the one-tier drawback.

questions.q: One-tier compilers, such as those for C/C++, produce efficient, target-specific code, but you need a separate compiler or compilation for each target platform.
questions.explain: That is the one-tier trade-off: efficient code tied to one platform, so each platform needs its own compiler or compilation.

questions.q: What is the intermediate VM code called in Java and Python?
questions.explain: Java and Python call it bytecode. C#/.NET calls its equivalent IL.

questions.q: On the Hack/Jack platform, which chain shows how a Jack program becomes executable code?
choices: Jack → compiler → VM code → VM translator → assembly → assembler → binary
Jack → VM translator → VM code → compiler → assembly → assembler → binary
Jack → compiler → assembly → VM translator → VM code → assembler → binary
Jack → assembler → VM code → compiler → binary
questions.explain: The compiler turns .jack files into .vm files. The VM translator turns those into a .asm file, and the assembler turns that into .hack binary that runs on the Hack computer.

questions.q: Which way of implementing the VM is used by Java, C#, Python, and Jack?
choices: Native: add hardware modules for the stack and primitive instructions for the VM commands
Emulation: a high-level program models the stack and segments as ADTs
Translation: each VM command becomes machine instructions that work on the host RAM
None: the source code is run directly, with no VM layer
questions.explain: Translation turns each VM command into machine-language instructions and uses an addressing contract to place the stack and segments in dedicated RAM areas. The VM translator in this chapter works this way.

questions.q: VM translators are generally much harder to write than compilers.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: VM translators are much simpler than compilers. That is why needing one VM translator per platform is an acceptable cost.

questions.q: How does a VM emulator differ from a VM translator?
choices: An emulator uses a high-level language to execute VM commands; a translator converts them into a target machine language
An emulator converts VM commands into a target machine language; a translator executes them directly
An emulator compiles Jack into VM code; a translator converts VM code into Jack
They are two names for the same program
questions.explain: Both implement the VM abstraction. The emulator runs VM programs directly and shows how the stack and segments sit in the host RAM. The translator produces machine code for a real platform.

questions.q: The stack holds 4, 9, 2 (bottom to top, 2 on top). After sub, what does it hold, bottom to top?
questions.explain: sub pops y = 2 (the top) and x = 9 (the value below it), then pushes x - y = 7. The 4 is untouched.

questions.q: Starting with an empty stack, run: push constant 3; push constant 10; sub. What value is on top of the stack?
questions.explain: x is the value pushed first (3) and y is the top (10). sub computes x - y = 3 - 10 = -7.

questions.q: Memory holds x = 6 and y = 3. Run: push constant 20; push x; sub; push y; neg; add; pop d. What is d?
questions.explain: 20 - 6 = 14. Pushing y and applying neg gives -3. 14 + (-3) = 11, and pop d stores it in d.

questions.q: Which VM sequence computes x - (y + 3)?
choices: push x; push y; push 3; add; sub
push x; push y; sub; push 3; add
push y; push 3; add; push x; sub
push x; push 3; push y; sub; sub
questions.explain: Push x, then compute y + 3 on top of it, then sub gives x - (y + 3). The second choice computes (x - y) + 3, the third (y + 3) - x, and the fourth x - (3 - y).

questions.q: Starting with an empty stack, run: push constant 5; push constant 6; push constant 7; add; neg. What value is on top of the stack?
questions.explain: add pops 6 and 7 and pushes 13, leaving 5, 13. neg replaces the top with -13.

questions.q: What does the stack pointer SP hold?
choices: The address of the topmost stack value
The address just after the topmost stack value (the next free slot)
The number of values currently on the stack
Always the stack's base address, 256
questions.explain: SP points to the RAM address just after the one holding the topmost value. That is why push writes to RAM[SP] and then increments SP, while pop decrements SP first.

questions.q: Every high-level arithmetic or logical expression can be translated into a sequence of VM commands operating on a stack.
questions.explain: This is why a stack machine is a suitable compilation target: any such expression becomes a sequence of pushes, operations, and pops.

questions.q: Which of these commands pop two operands from the stack?
choices: add
neg
gt
not
and
eq
questions.explain: add, sub, eq, gt, lt, and, and or are binary. neg and not are unary: they pop one value and push one result.

questions.q: After push constant 3; push constant 8; gt, the value on top of the stack is true.
questions.explain: gt computes x > y, where x is the value pushed first (3) and y is the top (8). 3 > 8 is false.

questions.q: In the Hack implementation of the VM, how are true and false represented?
choices: true = 1, false = 0
true = -1, false = 0
true = 0, false = -1
true = 1, false = -1
questions.explain: true is -1 (all bits set in 16-bit two's complement) and false is 0.

questions.q: x = 4 and y = 9. Run: push x; push constant 7; lt; push y; push constant 8; eq; or. Using the Hack representation of booleans, what value is left on the stack?
questions.explain: 4 < 7 is true, and 9 == 8 is false. true or false is true, which is -1 in the Hack implementation.

questions.q: Which VM command replaces the top value y with -y?
questions.explain: neg is the unary arithmetic command that computes -y. Do not confuse it with not, which is the logical complement.

questions.q: What does every arithmetic-logical VM command do?
choices: Pops as many operands as it needs, computes the operation, and pushes the result onto the stack
Reads the top operands without removing them and pushes the result above them
Pops its operands and stores the result in temp 0
Pops its operands and writes the result into the local segment
questions.explain: An n-argument operation pops n values, computes the function on them, and pushes the one result back onto the stack.

questions.q: According to the VM command table, which of these commands return an integer rather than a boolean?
choices: add
sub
neg
eq
and
not
questions.explain: add, sub, and neg return integers. eq, gt, lt, and, or, and not are listed as returning booleans.

questions.q: How many virtual memory segments does the VM architecture have?
questions.explain: The eight segments are local, argument, this, that, constant, static, temp, and pointer.

questions.q: A class declares static int s1, s2. Its method bar(int x, int y) declares var int a, b, c. Assume the compiler maps variables to segments in declaration order, starting at index 0. Which VM code implements a = s2 - x?
choices: push static 1; push argument 0; sub; pop local 0
push static 2; push argument 1; sub; pop local 1
push argument 0; push static 1; sub; pop local 0
push static 1; push local 0; sub; pop argument 0
questions.explain: s2 is static 1, x is argument 0, and a is local 0. Push s2 first so that sub computes s2 - x, then pop the result into a. The third choice computes x - s2.

questions.q: What is the temp segment for?
choices: Temporary variables the compiler generates that don't come from the source code
Local variables declared inside a subroutine
Static variables of a class
The base addresses of the this and that segments
questions.explain: Compilers sometimes need scratch variables of their own. temp is a fixed 8-entry segment, temp 0 through temp 7, for that purpose.

questions.q: Which segment holds the base addresses of the this and that segments, and comes into play when compiling code for objects and arrays?
choices: temp
pointer
static
constant
questions.explain: pointer has two entries. pointer 0 corresponds to THIS and pointer 1 to THAT.

questions.q: What does push constant i do?
choices: Pushes the integer i itself
Pushes the value stored at RAM[i]
Pushes entry i of the static segment
Pushes the value at address SP + i
questions.explain: The constant segment stands for the integers 0, 1, 2, ..., so constant i supplies the value i. No memory is read.

questions.q: In the VM abstraction, all eight segments are accessed the same way: push/pop segment i, where i is a non-negative integer.
questions.explain: All segments look and behave the same to VM code. Only their implementation on the host RAM differs.

questions.q: How many entries do the temp and pointer segments have?
choices: temp 8, pointer 2
temp 2, pointer 8
temp 16, pointer 2
temp 8, pointer 4
questions.explain: temp has 8 entries (temp 0 to temp 7). pointer has 2 (pointer 0 and pointer 1).

questions.q: In the standard VM mapping on Hack, at what RAM address does the stack start?
questions.explain: The stack occupies RAM[256] through RAM[2047].

questions.q: In the standard mapping, which RAM address holds temp 4?
questions.explain: temp i is stored at RAM[5 + i], so temp 4 is at RAM[9].

questions.q: Which RAM range holds the static variables?
questions.explain: 5–12 is temp, 13–15 is the general-purpose registers R13–R15, 16–255 is static, and 256–2047 is the stack.

questions.q: In order, what do RAM[0] through RAM[4] hold?
choices: SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT
SP, ARG, LCL, THIS, THAT
LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT, SP
SP, THIS, THAT, LCL, ARG
questions.explain: RAM[0] = SP, RAM[1] = LCL, RAM[2] = ARG, RAM[3] = THIS, RAM[4] = THAT.

questions.q: What are R13–R15 (RAM[13]–RAM[15]) for in the standard mapping?
choices: General-purpose registers the generated code can use for any purpose
The first three entries of the temp segment
The base addresses of local, argument, and this
Backup copies of the stack pointer
questions.explain: R13–R15 are predefined symbols that can be used for any purpose, for example to hold an address while translating pop.

questions.q: When translating the file Bar.vm, which assembly symbol does push static 5 refer to?
questions.explain: Static variable i in file Xxx.vm becomes the assembly symbol Xxx.i, so here it is Bar.5.

questions.q: Which program assigns the actual RAM addresses to the Xxx.i static symbols?
choices: The Hack assembler, which allocates variables starting at address 16
The VM translator, which hard-codes addresses starting at 256
The compiler, when it compiles the class
The OS, at run time
questions.explain: The VM translator only emits symbols such as Foo.3. The assembler later maps new variable symbols to RAM[16], RAM[17], and so on, which is exactly the static range.

questions.q: The standard mapping is the only possible way to realize the VM on the Hack platform.
questions.explain: The VM can be implemented in many ways. The standard mapping is a recommendation, and following it keeps you compatible with tools that use the same standard, such as VM emulators, OS routines, and test scripts.

questions.q: Which pseudocode implements pop local i?
choices: addr ← LCL + i; SP--; RAM[addr] ← RAM[SP]
addr ← LCL + i; RAM[addr] ← RAM[SP]; SP--
addr ← LCL + i; SP++; RAM[addr] ← RAM[SP]
addr ← LCL + i; RAM[SP] ← RAM[addr]; SP++
questions.explain: SP points one past the top value, so pop must decrement SP before reading RAM[SP]. The last choice is push local i.

questions.q: SP = 260, LCL = 1500, and RAM[259] = 42. After pop local 3, which RAM address holds 42?
questions.explain: addr = LCL + 3 = 1503. SP drops to 259, and RAM[1503] ← RAM[259] = 42.

questions.q: SP = 300, ARG = 400, and RAM[402] = 17. After push argument 2, what is the value of SP?
questions.explain: push writes RAM[300] ← RAM[ARG + 2] = 17 and then increments SP to 301.

questions.q: push constant 17 translates to: @17, D=A, @SP, A=M, M=D, @SP, M=M+1. What do the instructions @SP, A=M accomplish?
choices: They point A at the next free stack slot, so that M=D writes 17 there
They increment the stack pointer
They load the top stack value into D
They set SP to 17
questions.explain: @SP selects RAM[0]. A=M then loads the address stored in SP, so M now refers to RAM[SP], the next free slot. The final @SP, M=M+1 does the SP++.

questions.q: Which Hack assembly sequence correctly does 'SP--; D ← RAM[SP]', the first half of a pop?
choices: @SP, M=M-1, A=M, D=M
@SP, A=M, D=M, @SP, M=M-1
@SP, M=M+1, A=M, D=M
@SP, M=M-1, D=M
questions.explain: Decrement SP first, then use its new value as the address and read that cell into D. The second choice reads the empty slot above the top, the third moves SP the wrong way, and the fourth puts the address itself into D, not the value.

questions.q: How does the implementation of push/pop temp i differ from that of push/pop local i?
choices: temp uses the fixed address 5 + i; local uses the base address stored in LCL plus i
temp uses the base address stored in RAM[5]; local uses the fixed address 1 + i
They are identical: both read a base pointer from RAM
temp values live on the stack; local values live in the static area
questions.explain: temp is a fixed block at RAM[5..12], so push/pop temp i accesses RAM[5 + i] directly. local can be anywhere in RAM, so its base address must be read from LCL first.

questions.q: What does pop pointer 1 do?
choices: Pops the top value into THAT (RAM[4]), which sets the base address of the that segment
Pops the top value into THIS (RAM[3])
Pops the top value into RAM[THAT + 1]
Pops the top value into temp 1
questions.explain: pointer is not stored anywhere of its own. pointer 0 means THIS and pointer 1 means THAT, so pop pointer 1 means pop THAT.

questions.q: push/pop for argument, this, and that are implemented exactly like local, except that the base pointer is ARG, THIS, or THAT.
questions.explain: All four use addr ← segmentPointer + i, with LCL, ARG, THIS, or THAT as the segment pointer, and then move the value between RAM[addr] and the stack.

questions.q: For the command push local 3, what do the Parser routines return?
choices: commandType() = C_PUSH, arg1() = "local", arg2() = 3
commandType() = C_PUSH, arg1() = "push", arg2() = 3
commandType() = C_ARITHMETIC, arg1() = "local", arg2() = 3
commandType() = C_PUSH, arg1() = "local 3", no arg2()
questions.explain: The command keyword determines the type (C_PUSH). arg1 is the segment name as a string and arg2 is the index as an int.

questions.q: For the command add, what string does the Parser's arg1() return?
questions.explain: For C_ARITHMETIC commands, arg1 returns the command itself (add, sub, neg, ...).

questions.q: For which command types may the Parser's arg2() be called?
choices: C_PUSH
C_POP
C_ARITHMETIC
C_FUNCTION
C_CALL
C_RETURN
questions.explain: Only push, pop, function, and call have a second, integer argument. (arg1 should not be called for C_RETURN, since return has no arguments.)

questions.q: In the proposed translator design, what does the VMTranslator module do?
choices: Runs the process: creates a Parser for the input and a CodeWriter for the output, then loops over the input commands
Splits each VM command into its parts
Writes the assembly code for each command
Assembles the generated .asm file into binary
questions.explain: The Parser reads and splits commands, the CodeWriter generates assembly, and the VMTranslator coordinates the two.

questions.q: Which CodeWriter routine writes the assembly code for the sub command?
questions.explain: writeArithmetic(command) handles arithmetic-logical commands. writePushPop(command, segment, index) handles push and pop.

questions.q: To parse a VM command, the Parser needs to know what the command does.
questions.explain: Parsing deals only with syntax. The Parser identifies the command type and arguments, and the CodeWriter handles meaning.

questions.q: Translating Foo.vm produces which output file?
choices: Foo.asm
Foo.hack
Foo.out
Foo.cmp
questions.explain: The VM translator emits Hack assembly into fileName.asm. The assembler later turns that into .hack binary.

questions.q: The Parser ignores white space and // comments in the .vm file.
questions.explain: Comments, indentation, and white space are allowed in VM files and are skipped during parsing.

questions.q: What are the primitive data types of the basic Jack language?
choices: int, boolean, char
int, float, boolean
int, char, String
int, boolean, char, float
questions.explain: Jack has only int, boolean, and char. Other types are built as classes. This is why Point.distance returns an int, not a float.

questions.q: In Jack, what is a function, as opposed to a method or a constructor?
choices: A static subroutine that operates on no particular object
A subroutine that operates on the current object
A subroutine that creates a new object
A subroutine that only the OS can provide
questions.explain: Constructors create new objects, methods operate on the current object, and functions are static and operate on no particular object.

questions.q: A Jack constructor must explicitly return the memory address of the newly created object, which is denoted this.
questions.explain: That is why Point.new ends with 'return this;'.

questions.q: When a Jack program creates an object with new, how is a place in RAM found for it?
choices: An OS routine finds and allocates the memory
The compiler picks a fixed address at compile time
The VM translator reserves space on the stack
The assembler allocates it starting at address 16
questions.explain: The compiler does not know where the object will go. It generates a call to an OS memory-management routine that finds the space at run time.

questions.q: The Jack OS is written in Jack itself, much as Unix was developed in C. What is this development strategy called?
questions.explain: Bootstrapping means using a language to build the system software that the language itself relies on.

questions.q: In the Point class, how do the field variables x and y differ from the static variable pointCount?
choices: Each Point object has its own x and y; pointCount is one class-level variable shared by all Points
x and y are shared by all Points; each Point has its own pointCount
Fields are stored on the stack; static variables are stored in temp
There is no difference; field and static mean the same thing
questions.explain: Fields (also called properties or instance variables) belong to each object. A static variable belongs to the class as a whole, and the VM keeps it in the static segment.

questions.q: p1 = Point.new(1,2), p2 = Point.new(3,4), and p3 = p1.plus(p2). What does p1.distance(p3) return?
What are the compiler's two main tasks?
choices: Syntax analysis and code generation
Memory allocation and garbage collection
Assembly and linking
Emulating VM commands and drawing on the screen
questions.explain: The Jack compiler first analyzes the program's syntax, then generates VM code from it.
